questions.q: A nightly Spark job must finish as cheaply as possible and can safely retry failed tasks. Which EC2 purchase approach fits best?

options.t: On-Demand Instances in one instance type
options.why: Wrong: no discount; fine for uninterruptible work but the most expensive here.
Wrong: commitment suits a steady 24/7 baseline, not a nightly job.

options.t: Spot Instances across many instance types and AZs with price-capacity-optimized
options.why: Right: deep discount, interruptions only slow a retryable job, and more capacity pools mean fewer interruptions.
Wrong: a 1-3 year commitment pinned to one AZ is wasteful for a nightly job.

questions.explain: Fault-tolerant batch is the Spot use case.
questions.remember: Retryable or checkpointed batch work → Spot with many types/AZs and price-capacity-optimized. Never use Spot for databases or EMR primary/core nodes.
variants: Single long job with no checkpoint and a deadline → On-Demand (or Spot with fallback).
Steady 24/7 baseline → Savings Plans, not Spot.
Spot allocation strategy to avoid: lowest-price (highest interruption risk).

questions.q: A data platform has a steady 24/7 EC2 baseline for 3 years. The team may move some work to Fargate and Lambda, and may change Regions and instance families. Which commitment is best?

options.why: Right: applies to EC2 in any family, size, Region, OS and tenancy, and also to Fargate and Lambda.
Wrong: locked to one instance family in one Region, so it does not follow the move.
Wrong: tied to exact type and AZ, the least flexible.
Wrong: covers database services, not EC2.

questions.explain: Flexibility across services and Regions points to the Compute Savings Plan.
questions.remember: Need flexibility (Region, family, Fargate/Lambda) → Compute Savings Plan (up to 66%). Fixed family and Region → EC2 Instance Savings Plan (up to 72%).
variants: Baseline fixed on one family in one Region → EC2 Instance Savings Plan.
Need a capacity guarantee as well → add an On-Demand Capacity Reservation, because Savings Plans do not reserve capacity.
Discounts for RDS/DynamoDB → Database Savings Plans.

questions.q: A company must be sure that 50 instances can launch in one specific AZ for a 3-day migration window next month. It does not want a 1-3 year commitment. What should it use?

options.why: Wrong: gives a discount but does not reserve capacity.
Wrong: Regional RIs give a discount but no capacity reservation.
Wrong: Spot can be interrupted and capacity is never guaranteed.
Right: reserves capacity for a type, platform and AZ for any duration, with no term.

questions.explain: Only a Capacity Reservation guarantees capacity without a long term.
questions.remember: Guaranteed capacity in an AZ without a long commitment → On-Demand Capacity Reservation (billed whether or not it is used). Add Savings Plans for the discount.
variants: Guaranteed GPU capacity for a fixed future window for ML → Capacity Blocks for ML.
Capacity plus discount for steady load → Capacity Reservation plus Savings Plan or Regional RI.
Zonal RI also reserves capacity but needs a 1-3 year term.

questions.q: A team's EC2 bill rose unexpectedly after moving a steady, CPU-heavy workload to t3 instances. CPU stays above baseline for hours every day. What is the likely cause and fix?

options.t: Standard mode throttling; switch to Unlimited
options.why: Wrong: Standard mode only slows the CPU to baseline and adds no charge; T3 also launches as Unlimited by default.

options.t: Unlimited mode surplus credit charges; move the steady load to M or C instances
options.why: Right: bursting above baseline in Unlimited mode costs a flat rate per vCPU-hour (see CPUSurplusCreditsCharged).

options.t: Launch credits expired; buy more credits
options.why: Wrong: T3 has no launch credits and credits cannot be bought.
Wrong: unrelated to CPU burst behaviour.

questions.explain: Sustained CPU above baseline on a T instance in Unlimited mode costs extra.
questions.remember: T instance: Standard mode = slows down at no extra cost; Unlimited mode = keeps speed but pays surplus. Steady high CPU → M/C family instead.
variants: Job on a T2 (Standard) slows every night → credits exhausted; use Unlimited or a larger or fixed-performance type.
Metric to watch for surplus charges → CPUSurplusCreditsCharged.
T instances cannot be used in cluster placement groups.

questions.q: ETL instances in a private subnet read terabytes from S3 through a NAT gateway, and the NAT processing charges are very high. What is the best fix?

options.t: Add a second NAT gateway in another AZ
options.why: Wrong: adds an hourly fee and the per-GB processing still applies.

options.t: Move the instances to a public subnet with Elastic IPs
options.why: Wrong: adds public IPv4 cost and exposure, and does not remove the need for a clean design.

options.t: Add an S3 gateway VPC endpoint and route the subnet to it
options.why: Right: gateway endpoints are free and S3 traffic skips the NAT gateway.
Wrong: works, but has hourly and per-GB cost; the gateway endpoint is free for in-VPC access.

questions.explain: A gateway endpoint for S3 removes NAT processing fees.
questions.remember: Heavy S3 or DynamoDB traffic from private subnets → gateway endpoint (free, route table entry), not NAT.
variants: On-premises or another Region needs private S3 access → interface endpoint (PrivateLink), since gateway endpoints cannot be used from outside the VPC.
Bucket must accept only your VPC → aws:SourceVpce or aws:SourceVpc, not aws:SourceIp.
Big bill with 'Data Transfer' lines → check cross-AZ traffic as well.

questions.q: A self-managed Kafka and HDFS cluster on EC2 must place replicas on different racks so that one rack failure never removes all copies. Which placement group fits?

options.why: Wrong: packs instances close together for low latency, which concentrates failure risk.
Wrong: limited to 7 running instances per AZ per group, too small for a cluster.

options.t: No placement group; use several AZs only
options.why: Wrong: does not give rack awareness for replica placement.
Right: partitions sit on separate racks and instances can see their partition, so HDFS, HBase, Cassandra and Kafka can place replicas accordingly.

questions.explain: Rack-aware distributed systems use partition groups.
questions.remember: HDFS, HBase, Cassandra or Kafka rack awareness → partition (up to 7 partitions per AZ). Lowest latency → cluster. A few critical instances apart → spread (7 per AZ).
variants: Tightly coupled HPC or training needing lowest latency → cluster placement group plus EFA.
Three ZooKeeper nodes must not share hardware → spread placement group.
Burstable T instances cannot go into a cluster placement group.

questions.q: An EC2 instance fails the system status check because of an underlying host problem. The application needs the same instance ID and IP addresses back with no manual work. What helps?

options.t: Automatic recovery (simplified, on by default, or a CloudWatch alarm with the recover action)
options.why: Right: the instance is recovered on new hardware keeping its ID, private/public/Elastic IPs and EBS volumes.

options.t: Terminate the instance and launch a new one
options.why: Wrong: a new instance gets a new instance ID and new IPs.
Wrong: a reboot stays on the same failing host.
Wrong: security groups have nothing to do with host failure.

questions.explain: System check failures are fixed by recovery; instance check failures are not.
questions.remember: System status check fails → AWS host problem → recovery or stop/start. Instance status check fails → your OS problem; recovery does not help, fix or reboot it.
variants: Instance-store data after recovery → lost, together with RAM contents.
Instance status check fails (OOM, bad fstab) → fix the OS, use the Serial Console, or move the root volume.
Instance in an ASG that fails the checks → ASG terminates and replaces it.

questions.q: A web tier on EC2 must survive an AZ outage and must also replace instances that are running but whose application is returning errors. Which design is best?

options.t: An ASG in one AZ with EC2 status checks only
options.why: Wrong: one AZ is a single point of failure, and EC2 status checks do not see application errors.

options.t: An ASG across at least two AZs behind an ALB, with ELB health checks enabled on the ASG
options.why: Right: multi-AZ gives resilience; ELB health checks let the ASG replace instances whose app is broken.

options.t: A single large instance with automatic recovery
options.why: Wrong: one instance in one AZ is not highly available.

options.t: Two instances in the same AZ behind an ALB
options.why: Wrong: both fail together in an AZ outage.

questions.explain: Multi-AZ ASG plus ELB health checks.
questions.remember: High availability on EC2 = multiple instances across AZs behind a load balancer. Turn on ELB health checks in the ASG so broken apps are replaced.
variants: Instances replaced right after launch → grace period too short or wrong health check path.
Need fixed IPs for partners in front of the fleet → NLB with static IPs per AZ.
An unhealthy ASG instance is terminated and replaced, not rebooted.

questions.q: Worker instances process messages from an SQS queue. The fleet must grow and shrink with the amount of work waiting. Which scaling policy is best?

options.why: Wrong: only fits load that arrives at known times.

options.t: Simple scaling on CPU with a 300-second cooldown
options.why: Wrong: legacy policy, and CPU does not reflect queue backlog.

options.t: Target tracking on backlog per instance (visible messages divided by running instances)
options.why: Right: keeps the queue backlog per worker at a target as the queue grows or drains.
Wrong: not automatic.

questions.explain: Queue workers scale on backlog per instance.
questions.remember: Queue-driven ETL fleet → target tracking on SQS backlog per instance. Known daily start → scheduled (or predictive) scaling.
variants: Same load every night at 01:00 → scheduled scaling.
Regular daily and weekly cycles with slow boot → predictive scaling.
Several policies at once → the ASG uses the one giving the largest capacity.

questions.q: Application logs on ASG instances are lost whenever the group scales in. Which approach preserves them?

options.t: A termination lifecycle hook (Terminating:Wait) that copies logs to S3 before termination
options.why: Right: the hook pauses the instance so a script can drain work and copy logs off; streaming logs continuously with the CloudWatch agent also works.
Wrong: runs at launch, not at termination.
Wrong: instance store is erased on terminate.

options.t: Turn on termination protection on the instance
options.why: Wrong: does not stop ASG scale-in; ASGs use their own scale-in protection.

questions.explain: Use a terminate lifecycle hook or stream logs off the instance.
questions.remember: Need to do something before an ASG instance dies (copy logs, drain, deregister) → Terminating:Wait lifecycle hook (default 1 hour, max 48 hours). Or stream logs with the CloudWatch agent.
variants: Install software or register at launch → Pending:Wait hook.
Protect an instance running a long task from scale-in → ASG scale-in protection.
Take one instance out for maintenance without replacement → standby.

questions.q: A team encrypted an AMI's snapshots with the default aws/ebs key and now needs to let another AWS account launch instances from it. What must be done?

options.t: Share the AMI directly; the other account can use aws/ebs automatically
options.why: Wrong: AMIs encrypted with the default aws/ebs key cannot be shared.
Wrong: exposes the image and still does not fix the key issue.

options.t: Copy the AMI to another Region
options.why: Wrong: key problem remains and KMS keys are Regional.

options.t: Re-encrypt with a customer managed KMS key, share the AMI, and grant the other account use of the key
options.why: Right: only customer managed keys can be shared, and the other account also needs key permission.

questions.explain: Cross-account encrypted AMIs need a customer managed key plus key access.
questions.remember: Share encrypted AMI or snapshot cross-account → customer managed key, share the image, grant the key. Default aws/ebs cannot be shared.
variants: Same AMI in another Region → copy it, re-encrypting with a key in the destination Region.
Deregistering an AMI leaves its snapshots, which still cost money.
Block cross-Region copy for sovereignty → SCP on ec2:CopyImage / CopySnapshot.

questions.q: A security audit flags SSRF risk to instance role credentials. After the team enforces IMDSv2, containers running on the EC2 hosts can no longer obtain credentials. What fixes it?

options.why: Wrong: re-enables IMDSv1 and the SSRF risk.

options.t: Raise the metadata hop limit to 2
options.why: Right: the default hop limit of 1 stops the token response before it reaches containers behind a bridge network.

options.t: Open port 80 in the security group
options.why: Wrong: security groups do not filter IMDS traffic.
Wrong: apps then cannot get role credentials at all.

questions.explain: Containers need hop limit 2 for IMDSv2.
questions.remember: IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) defends against SSRF. Containers on EC2 (Docker bridge, EKS pods) → hop limit 2. Old SDKs using IMDSv1 must be updated.
variants: Enforce IMDSv2 across the org → SCP/IAM condition ec2:MetadataHttpTokens = required, plus the account-level default.
IMDSv2 token lifetime → 1 second to 6 hours.
Find remaining IMDSv1 calls → CloudWatch metric MetadataNoToken.

questions.q: Engineers need shell access to instances in private subnets with no inbound ports open, no bastion host and a full audit trail. Choose TWO actions.

options.t: Open port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0 and distribute shared SSH keys
options.why: Wrong: exposes SSH to the world and gives no per-user IAM control.

options.t: Use Session Manager, with the SSM Agent and an instance role that has AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore
options.why: Right: shell access through IAM with no inbound ports, bastion or keys.

options.t: Deploy a bastion host in a public subnet
options.why: Wrong: the question asks for no bastion host.

options.t: Send session logs to S3 or CloudWatch Logs (KMS-encrypted); API calls are recorded in CloudTrail
options.why: Right: gives the audit trail of who ran what.

questions.explain: Session Manager plus session logging.
questions.remember: Private instance access with audit → Session Manager (IAM, no inbound ports, logs to S3/CloudWatch Logs, calls in CloudTrail). Fully private subnets need SSM interface endpoints or NAT.
variants: SSH/RDP into private instances without bastion or public IP → EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint.
Session Manager cannot connect → agent not running, role missing AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore, or no path to SSM.
Boot or network problems when SSH fails → EC2 Serial Console.

questions.q: A security team wants to block one specific malicious IP range from reaching every instance in a subnet. Which control should they use?

options.why: Wrong: security groups only have allow rules.
Wrong: does not target one range and breaks legitimate access.

options.t: A network ACL deny rule on the subnet
options.why: Right: NACLs support deny rules, evaluated in number order, first match wins.
Wrong: route tables do not filter by source range for inbound traffic.

questions.explain: Only NACLs can deny.
questions.remember: Block a specific IP/range → NACL deny. Allow by app tier → security group referencing another SG. NACLs are stateless, so allow ephemeral ports 1024-65535 for replies.
variants: Outbound works but replies are dropped with a custom NACL → return ephemeral ports not allowed.
DB must accept only app servers even as the ASG scales → SG rule with the app SG as source.
New custom SG → no inbound, all outbound allowed.

questions.q: An application on EC2 needs a database password that rotates automatically, and no secret may be stored in the AMI, code or user data. What is the best design?

options.t: Read the password from Secrets Manager at runtime using the instance role
options.why: Right: Secrets Manager supports automatic rotation and the instance profile gives temporary credentials.

options.t: Put the password in user data
options.why: Wrong: user data is not encrypted and is readable through metadata and the API.

options.t: Bake the password into a golden AMI
options.why: Wrong: cannot rotate and leaks to anyone who can launch the AMI.

options.t: Store it in an access-key file on the instance
options.why: Wrong: long-lived keys on instances are never recommended.

questions.explain: Fetch secrets at runtime with the instance role.
questions.remember: Secrets on EC2 → Secrets Manager (rotation) or Parameter Store SecureString (KMS) read with the instance role. Never in code, AMI or user data.
variants: No rotation needed and cheaper → Parameter Store SecureString.
AWS access from the instance → IAM role via instance profile, never access keys.
Launch with a role fails with UnauthorizedOperation → caller needs iam:PassRole.

questions.q: A pipeline should scale out its EC2 workers when memory usage is high, but the team cannot find a memory metric in CloudWatch. What should they do?

options.t: Enable detailed monitoring and use MemoryUtilization
options.why: Wrong: detailed monitoring only changes the period to 1 minute; no memory metric exists.

options.t: Use CPUUtilization as a memory proxy only
options.why: Wrong: CPU does not reflect memory pressure.
Wrong: measures EBS I/O, not memory.

options.t: Install the CloudWatch agent and use mem_used_percent in the scaling policy
options.why: Right: memory, disk space and swap are not default metrics and come from the agent.

questions.explain: Memory and disk-used need the CloudWatch agent.
questions.remember: Default metrics (CPU, network, disk ops, status checks) come from the hypervisor. Memory, disk space, swap, processes and app logs need the CloudWatch agent (role with CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy).
variants: Out of disk not visible → agent disk_used_percent alarm, grow with Elastic Volumes.
Faster Auto Scaling reaction → detailed monitoring (1-minute).
Basic monitoring period → 5 minutes (free).

questions.q: An auditor asks who opened SSH to the world on a security group last week. Which service answers it?

options.why: Wrong: shows traffic metadata, not who changed the rule.
Right: records EC2 API calls with who, when and from where.
Wrong: scans for vulnerabilities and exposure, not API history.
Wrong: collects OS and app logs, not API calls.

questions.explain: CloudTrail records API calls.
questions.remember: Who did an EC2 API action → CloudTrail. What a resource looked like over time → AWS Config. Who talked to an instance → VPC Flow Logs.
variants: Continuously detect SGs open to 0.0.0.0/0 on SSH → AWS Config rule restricted-ssh with SSM remediation.
Rejected traffic analysis → VPC Flow Logs queried with Athena or Logs Insights.
Threats like crypto-mining or credential exfiltration → GuardDuty.

questions.q: A compliance rule says data must never leave approved Regions. Which control prevents copying AMIs and snapshots to other Regions?

options.why: Wrong: do not control API actions like copying images.
Wrong: protects data at rest, not where it is copied.

options.t: Organizations SCPs that deny actions in other Regions, including ec2:CopyImage and ec2:CopySnapshot
options.why: Right: SCPs on aws:RequestedRegion block the API calls account-wide.
Wrong: NACLs filter network traffic, not API calls.

questions.explain: Region-deny SCPs enforce data sovereignty.
questions.remember: Data sovereignty → SCP using aws:RequestedRegion, also blocking CopyImage, CopySnapshot and Backup copies to forbidden Regions.
variants: Require encrypted volumes everywhere → EBS encryption by default per Region plus SCP on ec2:Encrypted.
Require IMDSv2 → SCP on ec2:MetadataHttpTokens.
Detect non-compliance after the fact → AWS Config rules.

questions.q: A company runs software licensed per physical core and must report socket and core counts. Which EC2 option fits?

options.why: Right: a whole physical server where you see sockets and cores, with host affinity for BYOL.
Wrong: single-tenant but gives no visibility of sockets or cores.
Wrong: reserves capacity, not licensing visibility.
Wrong: interruptible and offers no licence control.

questions.explain: Per-socket or per-core licences need Dedicated Hosts.
questions.remember: BYOL tied to sockets or cores → Dedicated Host. Compliance needing only single-tenant hardware → Dedicated Instance (cheaper, simpler, plus a Regional fee).
variants: Dedicated Hosts do not support Capacity Reservations.
Dedicated Host Reservation → up to 70% off.
Dedicated Instance fee → $2/hour per Region with any running.

questions.q: A new account tries to launch 20 p5 GPU instances and the call fails with VcpuLimitExceeded. What should the team do?

options.why: Wrong: reservations also count against the vCPU quota.
Wrong: quotas are per Region, not per AZ.
Wrong: a discount does not change quotas.

options.t: Request a quota increase in Service Quotas for that family's vCPU limit
options.why: Right: On-Demand limits are counted in vCPUs per Region and some GPU families default to 0.

questions.explain: Quota errors are fixed in Service Quotas.
questions.remember: VcpuLimitExceeded / InstanceLimitExceeded → raise the Regional vCPU quota. InsufficientInstanceCapacity → AWS lacks capacity: other AZ/type, attribute-based selection, or ODCR.
variants: InsufficientInstanceCapacity in a cluster placement group → launch all at once with one type, stop/start the group, or reserve with ODCR.
Subnet out of IPs → InsufficientFreeAddressesInSubnet; use a larger subnet.
Stopped and hibernated instances do not count toward the quota; Capacity Reservations do.
